summary: Intermittent TTFB regressions for streaming completions when API gateway connection reuse interacts with proxy buffering
description:
Issue summary: Customer reports intermittent increases in time-to-first-byte (TTFB) for streaming completions. The symptom is that some streaming requests return initial tokens after a 2-6s delay even though request enters the serving runtime quickly. Impact: customers see perceived latency spikes for interactive flows and partial timeouts when clients have strict idle time windows. Observed at scale across multiple backends in us-west and reproduceable in limited cases from internal synthetic tests.

Observed behavior:
- Requests accepted by API gateway and routed to serving cluster immediately (backend request logs show sub-200ms queuing).
- First chunk from serving runtime often delayed by multiple seconds before being flushed to client. Subsequent chunks stream normally after first flush.
- When we disable proxy buffering on edge (apigw/nginx) the TTFB returns to expected ~120-300ms range.

Why this is likely: preliminary triage indicates a protocol/conn-reuse mismatch between API gateway (proxy) keepalive behaviour and the serving runtime's chunking strategy. When proxy buffering is enabled and the proxy reuses a keepalive connection that previously saw a large header/tracing payload, it sometimes buffers until either (a) a buffer threshold is reached, or (b) the backend explicitly flushes by closing or hitting a chunk boundary we do not trigger. This causes the first-chunk delay but not subsequent tokens once the stream is warmed.
steps_to_reproduce: 1) Use customer streaming API with small prompt (~80 tokens) against redwood/bison-2-7b in us-west.
2) Ensure client keeps a short idle timeout (2-5s) between request start and consuming first token.
3) Send 100 concurrent streaming requests over a reused keepalive connection from same client IP.
4) Observe distribution of TTFB; ~15-30% of requests exhibit 2-6s TTFB while others respond fast.
5) Toggle proxy_buffering off on the APIGW/nginx side and re-run; issue disappears in synthetic test.
6) Re-enable buffering and run with a clean TCP connection per request; TTFB regressions reduce substantially.

comments: 2026-03-10 - Aisha Khan (Support): Customer NimbleDocs reported frequent user-facing stalls starting 2026-03-08 after a traffic spike. Provided initial logs and sample request/response headers.
2026-03-10 - Diego Martinez (SRE): Reproduced with internal loadtest. Noticed correlation with connection reuse and presence of large trace headers. Opening investigation with edge team.

2026-03-11 - Priya Rao (Edge Eng): Found nginx proxy_buffering and proxy_http_version differences when connection reused after large header set. Suggested testing disabling proxy_buffering as quick mitigation.
2026-03-11 - Customer (NimbleDocs): Verified turning off 'proxy_buffering' in their test environment eliminated stalls in 200/200 samples.
2026-03-12 - Diego Martinez (SRE): Rolled a config change to disable proxy_buffering for streaming routes in canary; monitoring telemetry for regressions.
2026-03-12 - Aisha Khan (Support): Notified customer about temporary mitigation and ETA for permanent fix.
investigation_notes: Hypothesis 1: proxy_buffering combined with keepalive reuse causes proxy to wait for enough data or connection-close to flush first chunk. Evidence: disabling buffering returns normal TTFB.

Hypothesis 2: large tracing headers from upstream clients sometimes change buffer allocation path and push proxy into a different flush policy. Evidence: requests with >8KB combined headers show higher probability of stalls.
Telemetry: 95th percentile TTFB for streaming endpoints jumped from ~480ms to ~2.8s for a subset of connections with conn_reuse=true between 2026-03-08 and 2026-03-09.
Reproduced locally using nginx with proxy_buffering=on and proxy_http_version=1.1 vs off; behaviour matches customer reports.
Risk: disabling proxy_buffering increases upstream load and may expose backend to small write amplification; need to tune keepalive and buffer thresholds.
Follow-ups: add a low-risk canary for proxy_buffering=false on streaming routes, add metric for 'first_chunk_delay' to per-route dashboards, and audit header size distribution for customers.
resolution: Mitigation applied: disabled proxy_buffering for streaming routes in APIGW canary (rolled to 10% of edge hosts). Also aligned keepalive timeouts between APIGW (now 120s) and load balancer to avoid reuse windows that previously exposed the bug. Permanently: engineering will add an explicit backend flush hook for first-chunk emission and add a feature flag to prefer flush-on-first-chunk for streaming models. Customer notified and accepted workaround. Postmortem planned; estimated full rollout after performance validation.
next_steps: 1) Instrument first_chunk_delay metric and add alert at 1.5s for streaming endpoints
2) Implement explicit flush-on-first-chunk in serving-runtime (PR opened)
3) Run load test with proxy_buffering disabled at 50% edge capacity to measure upstream load impact
4) Communicate permanent fix ETA to NimbleDocs and update docs on streaming tuning
